title: Remember My favor
hook: the Children of Israel are reminded of the favors given them (2:40–47)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adam, told again, and your line: the story comes back deeper. Which detail did you notice this time? Adam's story ended with a promise of guidance. Today, a people who received it. Day three hundred forty.

Families keep certain stories for the hard nights. The time grandpa crossed a border with one suitcase. The winter the neighbors left food on the step. They aren't told for entertainment. They're told so nobody forgets who they are and what was done for them. Right after Adam, al-Baqarah turns and speaks directly to a family, the descendants of one man, Ya'qub, also called Israel. And it begins by telling their story back to them. Today: remember My favor.
screen: `STORIES FOR THE HARD NIGHTS.` → `SO NOBODY FORGETS.` → `A FAMILY HEARS ITS STORY BACK.`

segments.voice: Verse forty, in Pickthall's words: “O Children of Israel! Remember My favour wherewith I favoured you.” The Arabic word is ni'mah, a blessing, a grace given. And then the verse goes on: keep your covenant, and I will keep Mine. The next stretch of al-Baqarah, many pages of it, is that remembering. You were rescued from Pharaoh, who was killing your sons. The sea was parted for you. You were shaded with clouds in the desert, and fed with manna and quails. Water burst from a rock in twelve springs, one for each tribe. These are stories Jews also tell, from their own scripture, in their own words. The Qur'an tells them back with honor and with honesty: alongside the gifts, it remembers the calf, the grumbling, the broken promises, the way any family history includes both. Why would a book addressed to the whole world spend so long speaking to one people? Some commentators answer: because the pattern is for everyone. A community is given much, makes a covenant, remembers or forgets. Muslim teachers read these passages as a warning to Muslims too: the same favor, the same covenant, the same risk of forgetting. The first instruction isn't obey. It's remember. Gratitude, in this verse, is a kind of memory. A promise is hard to keep to someone whose kindness has been forgotten. Remember the favor, and the covenant becomes something you keep because you remember, not only because you're told.
screen: `NI'MAH: A FAVOR, A GRACE GIVEN` · `RESCUE, SEA, CLOUDS, MANNA` · `THE PATTERN IS FOR EVERYONE` · `GRATITUDE IS A KIND OF MEMORY`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list three favors given to you. Not general ones. Specific, with names and places. The teacher who stayed late. The stranger who found your wallet. The night someone drove two hours to sit with you. Bring the first one to mind and stay with it for a few breaths. Then the second. Then the third. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah after each. The bell holds the time.
Remember My favor. Al-Baqarah's call to the Children of Israel, which Muslim teachers read as a call to everyone: before keeping a covenant, remember what was given. Today's word.
Your line: remember the favor. Today, write down one of your three favors and, if you can, tell the person who gave it. Day three hundred forty.

howItsDone: Muslims read al-Baqarah's long address to the Children of Israel as part of the Qur'an's teaching to every community, and naming blessings aloud with alhamdulillah is a common habit.

what it means: a call to remember what was given, so the covenant can be kept.
what a scholar hears: the long address to Bani Isra'il in 2:40 onward, which commentators read as a pattern for every community, Muslims included.

notes: Pickthall's 2:40 opening quoted from memory, keeping his British spelling inside the quotation; please confirm.

Tone: the passage includes the Qur'an's criticisms (the calf, broken promises). The script mentions them as part of 'any family history' and frames the whole address as a lesson Muslim teachers apply to Muslims too. A Keeper should check that the framing is fair and never makes Jews a foil.
Twelve springs (2:60) and the parallel in Exodus 15:27/17:6: the Exodus parallels are general, not exact; confirm the phrase 'stories Jews also tell, from their own scripture'.
